stories.title: The Lions Roar Into the ASEAN Semi-Finals!
stories.headline_kid: Singapore's football team drew with Indonesia and is now unbeaten, marching proudly into the semi-finals of the ASEAN Championship!
summary: Singapore's national football team, nicknamed the Lions, played a thrilling match against Indonesia. When Indonesia scored first, it looked like trouble, but striker Ilhan Fandi fired back with an equalising goal to make it a 1-1 draw.
That single point was enough to send Singapore through to the semi-finals of the ASEAN football championship. Even better, the Lions have not lost a single match in the whole tournament so far!

Being unbeaten means the team has stayed strong through every game, like a student who has passed every test this term. Their next opponent in the semi-finals will be a tough test, but fans across Singapore are cheering them on.

This tournament matters because it brings together the best teams from Southeast Asia, and doing well shows how far Singapore football has come. Win or lose the semi-final, the Lions have already made the nation proud.

lenses.me: You might catch the semi-final on TV or hear classmates talking about it during recess.
lenses.family: Families might gather to watch the match together, cheering for the Lions as a team.
lenses.friends: Your friends might wear Singapore jerseys or talk excitedly about Ilhan Fandi's goal.
lenses.nation: A good tournament result boosts national pride and shows Singapore can compete with our neighbours in sport.
lenses.world: Southeast Asian countries get to show off their footballing talent and build friendly rivalry through the game.

stories.title: Singapore's Only Sake Brewery Makes History with Black Rice
stories.headline_kid: A Singaporean and a Japanese brewer teamed up in Jurong to make Singapore's very own sake — even using local black glutinous rice!
summary: Tucked inside a Jurong building full of seafood suppliers is a tiny but special space: Orchid Sake Brewery, Singapore's first and only sake brewery. Sake is a traditional Japanese rice wine, usually made in cool, quiet places in Japan — not in Singapore's hot, humid weather!

The brewery was started by Singaporean Reuben Oh and Japanese head brewer Yumika Yamamoto. They had to solve tricky problems, like keeping the rice fermenting at the right cool temperature even though Singapore is always warm.

Instead of copying Japan exactly, they created something new — sake made with pulut hitam, the black glutinous rice used in local desserts like bubur pulut hitam. This gives their sake a uniquely Singaporean flavour that no one else in the world makes.
Their hard work has paid off. The sake is now served at Michelin-starred restaurants, has won awards in international competitions, and is even recognised in Japan, the birthplace of sake itself.

lenses.me: It shows that you can take something from another culture and make it your own with creativity and hard work.
lenses.family: Families might get curious and try local food and drink innovations like this when eating out.
lenses.friends: Your friends might be surprised to learn Singapore has its own sake, made right here at home.
lenses.nation: It's a proud example of Singaporean creativity being recognised on the world stage, blending cultures into something new.
lenses.world: It shows how food and drink traditions can travel across countries and be reinvented in exciting ways.

stories.title: Fires Blaze Near Mount Bromo as Dry Season Bites
stories.headline_kid: Firefighters in Indonesia are battling a big wildfire near the famous Mount Bromo volcano, as a dry weather pattern called El Nino makes things worse.
summary: A wildfire has been burning through Mount Bromo National Park on Indonesia's Java island, destroying more than 120 hectares of land — that's roughly the size of over 200 football fields! Firefighters and two water-bombing helicopters have been working hard to put out the flames.

The fire is getting worse because of El Nino, a natural weather pattern that starts in the Pacific Ocean and can make some parts of Southeast Asia much hotter and drier than usual, almost like turning up an oven. Dry plants and grass catch fire more easily during these conditions.

This matters for Singapore too. When land and forest fires burn in our region, especially in Indonesia, smoke can sometimes drift over and cause haze here, making the air hazy and harder to breathe for some people.

Singapore's weather agencies are already keeping a close watch on the situation, just in case the smoke travels our way in the coming weeks. It's a good reminder to check air quality readings if the sky looks unusually smoky.

lenses.me: If haze reaches Singapore, you might need to stay indoors more or wear a mask during outdoor PE lessons.
lenses.family: Families may need to check the air quality app before planning outdoor activities like picnics or sports.
lenses.friends: Outdoor school events like sports day could be affected if haze becomes bad enough.
lenses.nation: Singapore monitors regional fires closely because haze affects health, schools, and even flights.
lenses.world: It shows how weather patterns like El Nino can affect many countries at once, not just where the fire is burning.

stories.title: Thai Students Mourn After a Shocking School Tragedy
stories.headline_kid: A sad and shocking event happened at a school near Bangkok, where a young student caused great harm before losing his own life — and it reminds everyone how important it is to talk about our feelings.
summary: A very sad event happened at a school near Bangkok, Thailand's capital. A 14-year-old student, who people said had been struggling with bullying and other difficulties, brought a gun that belonged to his grandfather to school and caused harm to several teachers and staff members. Sadly, he also lost his own life.

Students at the school were left in shock and grief. Many hugged each other and cried, comforting one another through this frightening experience. Losing teachers and staff members who cared for them was a heavy blow to the whole school community.

This story is upsetting, but it teaches an important lesson: when someone feels overwhelmed, angry, or hurt inside — like a cup filling up with too much water — it's important they get help before things get worse. Schools, parents, and friends all play a part in noticing when someone needs support.

In Singapore, schools have been working on ways to help students who feel troubled, and to keep everyone safe. If you or a friend ever feels very upset or unsafe, telling a trusted adult — a parent, teacher, or school counsellor — is always the right thing to do.

lenses.me: It's a reminder to speak up if you ever feel overwhelmed, and to be kind to classmates who seem lonely or troubled.
lenses.family: Parents may want to talk with you about who you can turn to if you ever feel unsafe or upset.
lenses.friends: It's a chance to check in on friends who seem quiet, sad, or left out, and to include them.
lenses.nation: Singapore schools continue to strengthen counselling support and safety measures to protect students.
lenses.world: Communities everywhere are reminded that supporting young people's mental health can help prevent tragedies.

stories.title: Why Is Japan Building Up Its Military?
stories.headline_kid: Japan says it needs a stronger military because of growing tensions with China, North Korea, and Russia — and it matters for peace in our region too.
summary: Japan's Defence Minister, Shinjiro Koizumi, has urged his country to build up its defence forces with more urgency. Think of it like a family deciding to strengthen the locks on their house because they've noticed more strangers walking around the neighbourhood.

A new government report explained that Japan feels more threatened by three countries: China, North Korea, and Russia. These countries have been growing their own militaries and sometimes acting in ways that worry their neighbours, like conducting military exercises close to Japan's waters.

This isn't just Japan's problem. Southeast Asia, including Singapore, relies on peace and stability in the wider Asia-Pacific region for trade — many of the goods we buy, from electronics to food, travel through busy shipping routes in this part of the world.

Singapore has always taken a careful, friendly approach with all countries, big or small, hoping that talking and cooperation can solve problems instead of military build-ups. Still, when big countries tighten their defences, it's something worth understanding, since a peaceful region benefits everyone, including us.

lenses.me: You might hear grown-ups discussing this on the news, since it affects how countries in our region get along.
lenses.family: Your family's daily goods, from electronics to fruit, often travel by ships passing through Asia's waters, which need to stay peaceful.
lenses.friends: You and your friends can learn that countries, like people, sometimes feel the need to protect themselves when they feel worried.
lenses.nation: Singapore relies on regional peace for trade and safety, so tensions between big countries are always watched closely.
lenses.world: It shows how actions by powerful countries can ripple outward and affect the security plans of their neighbours.
